::: {.notes}
Open with the concrete behavior, not a sales claim. The audience is looking at a
normal Shiny-style control surface inside an MCP client. The controls collect
inputs, the client calls an R tool, and the card updates with R-computed
outputs. Set the credibility frame early: open source, experimental, not on
CRAN, synthetic data throughout. Then outline the structure: MCP, MCP Apps,
shinymcp, MCP clients, Shiny integration, and validation boundaries.
:::

## The integration gap

- You have R packages, Shiny apps, and clinical tools your team has reviewed
- MCP-capable clients are external to the R code your team owns
- Reimplementing the same logic for each client creates drift, review burden, and vendor-specific code

. . .

[Goal: let MCP clients call reviewed R tools without moving the computation out of R.]{.takeaway}

::: {.notes}
Name the actual gap. This audience does not need to be convinced Shiny is useful. They need a credible path from existing R assets into the MCP clients their teams are evaluating. The costly issue is duplicated clinical logic and duplicated validation. The claim is that R can stay the computation layer while MCP clients get a declared way to call it.
:::

## When to use shinymcp {.smaller}

[Reuse instead of rebuild. Keep your R code the computation layer, and expose it across MCP clients, Shiny, and shinychat.]{.takeaway}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {style="border-left:5px solid #087443; padding-left:1rem;"}
**Use shinymcp when**

- One named task you can call — screen a safety signal, summarize a cohort
- A fixed set of typed controls — dropdowns, numbers, sliders, checkboxes
- A result you can hand back — a plot, table, text, HTML, or image, plus a data object for the client
- Reuse across surfaces — one definition for MCP clients, an embedded Shiny card, and shinychat
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {style="border-left:5px solid #ff7518; padding-left:1rem;"}
**Avoid shinymcp when**

- Open-ended exploration — no single task to name with declared arguments
- It needs instant feedback — dragging a slider, brushing points, a live-streaming plot
- The interactive view *is* the deliverable — a rotatable 3-D plot, a hover-to-explore network
- State accumulates across steps — a multi-step wizard, not a one-shot call
:::
:::
:::

::: {style="color:#455468; margin-top:0.75rem; font-size:0.82em;"}
shinymcp is open source and experimental — pre-1.0, not yet on CRAN. All demo data is synthetic.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the spine of the talk. State the goal plainly: not to admire the package,
but to leave able to judge one of your own workflows. Give the WHY in one line —
reuse, don't rebuild — and preview the WHEN as two short lists. Say the maturity
caveat out loud here too: experimental, pre-1.0, not on CRAN, synthetic data. Do
not over-explain; the mechanism, the code, and the demo are what earn this
judgment. We return to this exact split near the close.
:::

# Why MCP {.section-divider background-color="#1b2f44"}

## MCP in Brief

- **One open standard** like a USB-C port for AI: connect once, reach any MCP client
- **MCP client:** the AI app (Claude, ChatGPT, Copilot, VS Code)
- **MCP server:** your process exposing approved **tools** (named functions with declared inputs) and **resources** (addressable context or UI assets)

```{=html}

  <div class="dgm-hub">
    <div class="dgm-hub__side left">

      <div class="row"><div class="dgm-node is-blue"><span class="k">CHAT</span><span class="t">Chat interfaces</span><span class="s">Claude · ChatGPT</span></div><div class="dgm-arr bi"><span class="ln"></span></div></div>

      <div class="row"><div class="dgm-node is-blue"><span class="k">AGENTS</span><span class="t">Other AI apps</span><span class="s">MCP-capable</span></div><div class="dgm-arr bi"><span class="ln"></span></div></div>
    </div>
    <div class="dgm-hub__core">

      <div class="row"><div class="dgm-node is-green"><span class="k">SYSTEMS</span><span class="t">Dev & enterprise</span><span class="s">Git · internal APIs</span></div><div class="dgm-arr bi green"><span class="ln"></span></div></div>
```

::: {.notes}
Keep the protocol explanation concrete. The picture mirrors the one on the MCP site: a column of AI applications on the left, the protocol in the middle, your tools and data on the right. MCP is the standard plug between them — the "USB-C for AI" line is the MCP docs' own framing, and it lands for this audience: build the connection once and any MCP client can use it. The client does not need to know R; it sees named tools, typed schemas, resources, and results. Foreshadow the rest of the talk: shinymcp is how your reviewed R and Shiny become one of those green boxes on the right.
:::

## The protocol layer is JSON messages

MCP separates **what** is requested from **how** bytes move.

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```json
{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 2,
  "method": "tools/call",
  "params": {
    "name": "explore_penguins",
    "arguments": {
      "species": "Gentoo",
      "x_var": "flipper_length_mm"
    }
  }
}
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Message shape: **JSON-RPC 2.0**
- Local transport: **stdio**
- Remote transport: **HTTP**
- Server process: **can be R**
- Tool contract: **name + schema + result**
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the technical grounding slide. MCP is not a browser framework and not a
client plugin API. It is a message protocol. The same `tools/call` semantics can
move over stdio, where the client launches Rscript as a subprocess, or over HTTP.
shinymcp's HTTP transport is JSON-RPC over POST; MCP's full Streamable HTTP
(server-sent events plus sessions) is a richer remote transport for later.
For this talk, the important point is that R can be the MCP server process and
the protocol boundary is a JSON message with a method, id, and params.
:::

## Discovery happens before calls

The client first asks what the R process exposes:

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
```json
{
  "method": "tools/list"
}
```

```json
{
  "name": "explore_penguins",
  "inputSchema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "species": { "type": "string" },
      "trend": { "type": "boolean" }
    }
  }
}
```
:::
::: {.column width="52%"}
```json
{
  "method": "tools/call",
  "params": {
    "name": "explore_penguins",
    "arguments": {
      "species": "Adelie",
      "trend": true
    }
  }
}
```
:::
:::

[For an R team, the schema is the reviewable boundary.]{.takeaway}

::: {.notes}
This is where R users should connect the protocol back to function signatures.
Before a tool is called, the client can discover the tool's name, description,
and input schema. The call then supplies arguments. That maps cleanly to how we
already reason about R functions: the name, formal arguments, defaults, and
return value are reviewable.
:::

## Why MCP might matters to you

- One **declared contract**, instead of client-specific glue
- Tool calls have names, schemas, arguments, and results you can inspect
- Open ecosystem path: build once, integrate across MCP clients as support matures
- Cleaner than asking a client to interpret a rendered dashboard

. . .

[MCP is a standard way to expose your tools and expertise to Claude or other MCP clients.]{.takeaway}

::: {.notes}
Translate MCP into pharma language. This is about exposing reviewed analytical
tools through a reviewable protocol. The key contrast is protocol call versus
dashboard interpretation. A protocol call is easier to inspect. Be precise that
client support varies; the contract is the portable part.
:::

# What MCP Apps add {.section-divider background-color="#1b2f44"}

## Tool vs MCP App: callable function plus interaction

- **Plain MCP tool**: client calls a named function → gets a return value
- **MCP App**: that same tool points to an app resource the user can touch
- The card is wired to the **same tool call**; it is not a passive screenshot

```{=html}
<div class="dgm-lanes">
  <div class="dgm-group">
    <span class="gl">Plain MCP tool</span>
    <div class="dgm-flow">
      <div class="dgm-node is-blue"><span class="k">MCP CLIENT</span><span class="t">Client</span></div>
      <div class="dgm-arr"><span class="lab">tools/call</span><span class="ln"></span></div>
      <div class="dgm-node is-green"><span class="k">TOOL</span><span class="t">screen_safety_signal()</span></div>
      <div class="dgm-arr back"><span class="lab">returns</span><span class="ln"></span></div>
      <div class="dgm-node"><span class="k">RESULT</span><span class="t">Value</span></div>
    </div>
  </div>
  <div class="dgm-group is-accent">
    <span class="gl">MCP App (adds an app resource)</span>
    <div class="dgm-flow">
      <div class="dgm-node is-blue"><span class="k">MCP CLIENT</span><span class="t">Client</span></div>
      <div class="dgm-arr"><span class="lab">tools/call</span><span class="ln"></span></div>
      <div class="dgm-node is-green"><span class="k">TOOL</span><span class="t">screen_safety_signal()</span></div>
      <div class="dgm-arr dashed"><span class="lab">_meta.ui.resourceUri</span><span class="ln"></span></div>
      <div class="dgm-node is-blue"><span class="k">RESOURCE</span><span class="t">app card</span><span class="s">inputs + outputs</span></div>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>
```

> Same function. App resource attached. Same tool contract.

::: {.notes}
Explain the mechanism plainly. A normal MCP tool is a callable function. An MCP
App attaches an addressable app resource to that tool. The card is active: user
interactions go back through the same inspectable tool call. The existing
analysis function becomes the tool; the UI becomes an interaction layer.
:::

## MCP App plumbing: tool descriptor + app resource

The tool says where the card lives; the resource returns the card HTML.

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```json
{
  "name": "explore_penguins",
  "inputSchema": { "type": "object" },
  "_meta": {
    "ui": {
      "resourceUri": "ui://penguins/app.html"
    }
  }
}
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```json
{
  "method": "resources/read",
  "params": {
    "uri": "ui://penguins/app.html"
  }
}
```

```text
text/html;profile=mcp-app
```
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Introduce `ui://` only now, after the room understands resources. It is just an
address for the app view, not a web URL the browser fetches directly. The tool
descriptor links to the resource. The client reads that resource and renders the
returned HTML as an MCP App. In shinymcp, the R package serves both: the tool and
the app resource.
:::

## What happens when someone touches the card

The card behaves like a small Shiny module with a different transport:

1. The user changes inputs.
2. The bridge turns those values into tool arguments.
3. The host sends `tools/call` to the MCP server.
4. R computes and returns display patches + result data.
5. The host sends the result back to the card.

```{=html}
<div class="dgm dgm-cycle">
  <div class="dgm-flow">
    <div class="dgm-node is-blue">
      <span class="k">USER</span>
      <span class="t">changes card inputs</span>
    </div>
    <div class="dgm-arr"><span class="lab">arguments</span><span class="ln"></span></div>
    <div class="dgm-node">
      <span class="k">MCP CLIENT</span>
      <span class="t">tools/call</span>
      <span class="s">name + args</span>
    </div>
    <div class="dgm-arr green"><span class="lab">runs</span><span class="ln"></span></div>
    <div class="dgm-node is-green">
      <span class="k">R</span>
      <span class="t">function computes</span>
    </div>
  </div>
  <div class="dgm-flow">
    <div class="dgm-node is-orange">
      <span class="k">DISPLAY</span>
      <span class="t">memo / table / plot</span>
      <span class="s">for the human</span>
    </div>
    <div class="dgm-arr back"><span class="lab">updates</span><span class="ln"></span></div>
    <div class="dgm-node is-green">
      <span class="k">RESULT DATA</span>
      <span class="t">result data</span>
      <span class="s">for logs, summaries, routing</span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
This is the core mechanism for people who know Shiny but not web protocols. In Shiny,
input changes update server state over a Shiny connection. In an MCP App, the
card is a small HTML view. shinymcp's bridge reads the inputs, packages them as
tool arguments, asks the host to call the R-backed tool, then writes the result
back into the card. The important point is the round trip: input values become an
inspectable tool call, not hidden browser behavior.
:::

## No Shiny.js, no server: names matching ids

- Inside an MCP client there is **no Shiny server and no Shiny.js**
- shinymcp ships ~800 lines of **dependency-free ES5 JS** — no npm build
- The bridge matches tool **argument names** to DOM element **ids**

. . .

**Contract:** arg name `==` input id · result key `==` output id

```{=html}
<div class="dgm">
  <div class="dgm-map">
    <div class="head">Tool schema (R)</div><div></div><div class="head r">DOM (HTML)</div>
    <div class="chip l">cohort</div><div class="eq"><span>==</span></div><div class="chip r">select#cohort</div>
    <div class="chip l">ae_term</div><div class="eq"><span>==</span></div><div class="chip r">input#ae_term</div>
    <div class="chip l">grade_threshold</div><div class="eq"><span>==</span></div><div class="chip r">input#grade_threshold</div>
    <div class="chip l">risk_limit</div><div class="eq"><span>==</span></div><div class="chip r">input#risk_limit</div>
  </div>
  <div class="dgm-cap">no Shiny.js — the bridge matches arg names to element ids</div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
The bridge reads the tool argument names, finds inputs whose ids match, and connects them. That replaces the Shiny.js websocket pattern for this narrow use case. The bridge is inspectable vanilla JS. Honest caveat: the binding is convention-based, so a typo can break the mapping; the bridge warns when an argument does not map to an input. The mcp_*() components exist to keep names aligned. Native shiny::selectInput("cohort") also works.
:::

# Convert a small Shiny app {.section-divider background-color="#1b2f44"}

## Toy app: one reactive group

```r
ui <- fluidPage(
  selectInput("species", "Species", c("All", "Adelie", "Gentoo")),
  selectInput("x_var", "X axis", names(penguins)),
  selectInput("y_var", "Y axis", names(penguins)),
  checkboxInput("trend", "Show trend line"),
  plotOutput("scatter"),
  verbatimTextOutput("stats")
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  filtered <- reactive({
    data <- palmerpenguins::penguins |> tidyr::drop_na()
    if (input$species != "All") data <- data[data$species == input$species, ]
    data
  })
  output$scatter <- renderPlot(plot_penguins(filtered(), input$x_var, input$y_var, input$trend))
  output$stats <- renderPrint(summary(filtered()[, c(input$x_var, input$y_var, "species")]))
}
```

::: {.notes}
Use the toy app because the room already understands it from the opener. There
is one reactive island: four inputs, one filtering reactive, and two outputs.
That is the easiest case for conversion because all outputs depend on the same
input set. The goal is not to teach Palmer Penguins; it is to make the Shiny to
MCP mapping concrete.
:::

## First pass: high-level helpers

```r
# In-memory app object: useful while iterating
penguins_app <- shinyApp(ui, server)
mcp <- as_mcp_app(penguins_app, name = "penguins-explorer", selective = FALSE)

# Source directory: useful when you want generated files to inspect
convert_app(
  "penguins-shiny",
  output_dir = "penguins-mcp",
  mode = "scaffold"
)
```

```text
penguins-mcp/
  ui.R       # card UI: controls + output placeholders
  tools.R    # tool schema + placeholder handler
  server.R   # MCP server entrypoint pieces
  app.R      # mcp_app(ui, tools, name = ...)
```

::: {.notes}
Call these the high-level helpers rather than selling them as a black box. They are
useful entry points, but the next slide opens the box. `as_mcp_app()` is useful
for an app object while iterating. `convert_app()` is useful when you want files
on disk and a reviewable scaffold. Stress that generated handlers are a starting
point; the reviewed computation still needs to be written or supplied.
:::

## What conversion extracts

`parse_shiny_app()` turns Shiny source into a small intermediate representation.

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
```r
ir <- parse_shiny_app("penguins-shiny")
```

```text
inputs:   species, x_var, y_var, trend
outputs:  scatter, stats
reactive: filtered()
refs:     input$species, input$x_var,
          input$y_var, input$trend
```
:::
::: {.column width="52%"}
```{=html}
<div class="dgm">
  <div class="dgm-flow">
    <div class="dgm-node"><span class="k">SOURCE</span><span class="t">app.R</span></div>
    <div class="dgm-arr"><span class="lab">parse</span><span class="ln"></span></div>
    <div class="dgm-node is-blue"><span class="k">IR</span><span class="t">ShinyAppIR</span><span class="s">inputs · outputs · refs</span></div>
  </div>
</div>
```
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
This is deliberately not a web-dev concept. The parser reads R source and
extracts the pieces R users already know: input IDs, output IDs, reactives, and
input references. It also classifies app complexity. For the toy app, this IR is
small enough to inspect by eye.
:::

## What the analyzer decides

`analyze_reactive_graph()` groups connected inputs and outputs into one tool.

```{=html}
<div class="dgm">
  <div class="dgm-flow">
    <div class="dgm-node is-blue"><span class="k">INPUTS</span><span class="t">species · x_var · y_var · trend</span></div>
    <div class="dgm-arr"><span class="lab">feed</span><span class="ln"></span></div>
    <div class="dgm-node"><span class="k">REACTIVE</span><span class="t">filtered()</span></div>
    <div class="dgm-arr green"><span class="lab">drives</span><span class="ln"></span></div>
    <div class="dgm-node is-green"><span class="k">TOOL</span><span class="t">explore_penguins()</span><span class="s">scatter + stats</span></div>
  </div>
</div>
```

```r
analysis <- analyze_reactive_graph(ir)
analysis$tool_groups[[1]]
```

```text
input_args: species, x_var, y_var, trend
outputs:    scatter, stats
```

::: {.notes}
This is the important conversion step. The analyzer is not trying to understand
penguin biology. It is building a dependency graph: which inputs are connected
to which reactives and outputs. One connected component becomes one tool. If an
app has independent reactive islands, card mode can split them.
:::

## What you review in the scaffold

The generated scaffold gives structure; the team supplies the reviewed body.

```r
explore_penguins <- function(species = "All",
                             x_var = "flipper_length_mm",
                             y_var = "body_mass_g",
                             trend = FALSE) {
  data <- palmerpenguins::penguins |> tidyr::drop_na()
  if (species != "All") data <- data[data$species == species, ]

  list(
    scatter = mcp_result_plot(
      function() print(plot_penguins(data, x_var, y_var, trend)),
      model_value = list(n = nrow(data), species = species)
    ),
    stats = mcp_result_text(
      penguin_stats(data, x_var, y_var),
      model_value = list(x_var = x_var, y_var = y_var)
    )
  )
}
```

::: {.notes}
This is where we should be precise about automation. The converter can infer the
shape of the contract: arguments and output keys. It should not pretend to
validate the statistical meaning of the function. The reviewed R body is where
teams keep control. The result keys still match the output IDs, and model_value
is the client-readable result data.
:::

## Scaling up: several reactive islands

Card mode splits one dashboard's independent workflows into separate MCP App scaffolds.

```r
convert_app(
  "safety-dashboard",
  output_dir = "safety-dashboard-mcp",
  mode = "cards",
  selective = TRUE,
  max_inputs_per_card = 5
)
```

```text
safety-dashboard-mcp/
  01-safety-signal/
  02-enrollment-rescue/
  03-data-quality-check/
  CONVERSION_NOTES.md
```

[The output is a review queue, not a finished conversion: generated cards, generated schemas, and notes. A human still supplies and reviews each tool body.]{.takeaway}

**Watch for:** dynamic UI · file uploads/downloads · observers with side effects · session state or hidden globals — these need review, not just scaffolding.

::: {.notes}
Answer the portfolio question while the conversion mechanics are still fresh.
Card mode splits independent reactive islands into smaller MCP App scaffolds, each
with its own schema and conversion notes. It does not validate arbitrary clinical
logic or side effects; the output is a review queue, and a human fills and reviews
each tool body.
:::

# Serve to MCP clients {.section-divider background-color="#1b2f44"}

## Claude/Copilot path: R is the backend {.runtime-slide}

```{=html}
<div class="runtime-visual">
  <div class="runtime-track">
    <div class="runtime-card is-blue">
      <span>01 MCP HOST</span>
      <strong>Claude Desktop / VS Code Copilot</strong>
      <em>chat UI, tool approval, MCP connection</em>
    </div>
    <div class="runtime-wire"><b>starts or connects</b></div>
    <div class="runtime-card is-green">
      <span>02 SERVER PROCESS</span>
      <strong>Rscript app.R</strong>
      <em><code>serve(app)</code> speaks MCP</em>
    </div>
    <div class="runtime-wire"><b>JSON-RPC</b></div>
    <div class="runtime-card is-ink">
      <span>03 CONTRACT</span>
      <strong>tools + resources</strong>
      <em>schemas, calls, <code>ui://</code> HTML</em>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="runtime-split">
    <div class="runtime-pane is-js">
      <span>HTML CARD</span>
      <strong>JavaScript bridge in the app view</strong>
      <ul>
        <li>reads input elements</li>
        <li>sends <code>tools/call</code> through the host</li>
        <li>patches outputs when results return</li>
      </ul>
    </div>
    <div class="runtime-pane is-r">
      <span>R PROCESS</span>
      <strong>shinymcp server + your R function</strong>
      <ul>
        <li>answers <code>tools/list</code> and <code>resources/read</code></li>
        <li>runs <code>app$call_tool()</code></li>
        <li>formats display output plus result data</li>
      </ul>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="runtime-loop">
    <i>input change</i><i>postMessage</i><i>tools/call</i><i>R computes</i><i>result updates card</i>
  </div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
This answers the common "is it JS or R?" question visually. In an MCP client
path, the host application owns the chat surface and the MCP connection. The
server process can be `Rscript app.R`; `serve(app)` is the MCP server. The HTML
card contains JavaScript, but that bridge coordinates the UI round trip. The
computation remains in R. For Copilot/VS Code, MCP Apps can render inline when
the server and host support them; for any client, the tool contract is the
stable part.
:::

## Claude/Copilot path: the details {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
```r
# app.R
app <- mcp_app(ui, tools, name = "safety-signal")
serve(app) # stdio by default
```

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "safety-signal": {
      "command": "Rscript",
      "args": ["/path/to/app.R"]
    }
  }
}
```
:::
::: {.column width="52%"}
- The MCP host launches or connects to the R server process
- `initialize`, `tools/list`, and `resources/list/read` describe what R exposes
- `tools/list` includes the tool schema and the app resource URI
- `resources/read` returns HTML with the shinymcp bridge embedded
- The bridge sends UI changes back as `tools/call`
- `tools/call` runs the R function and returns MCP content plus structured result data
- Inline app rendering depends on the client; the R-backed tool remains callable
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Keep this as the technical slide after the visual. Local clients usually start
the server command, so the command can be `Rscript`. The R process handles the
MCP protocol over stdio by default. The card is an HTML resource, not a second
R backend. The bridge JavaScript is necessary because the embedded card needs a
browser-side way to read inputs and update outputs. The actual tool body is
ordinary R.
:::

## What an MCP client sees

```r
# app.R
app <- mcp_app(ui = ui, tools = list(tool), name = "rpharma-safety-signal")
serve(app)  # stdio MCP server by default
```

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "rpharma-safety-signal": {
      "command": "Rscript",
      "args": ["/path/to/app.R"]
    }
  }
}
```

::: {.notes}
Use a local client config as the concrete example without making any one client
the headline. An MCP client launches an MCP server command; that command can be
Rscript. The R process exposes tools and resources. Be precise: the tool
contract is the stable cross-client piece; interactive UI rendering depends on
the client and connector mode.
:::

# Code: the contract {.section-divider background-color="#1b2f44"}

## Code 1 — the inputs and outputs (real code)

```r
# Inputs — these ids become the tool's argument names
mcp_select("cohort", "Cohort", cohort_choices)
mcp_select("ae_term", "AE term", ae_terms)
mcp_numeric_input("grade_threshold", "Minimum grade",
                  value = 3, min = 1, max = 4, step = 1)
mcp_numeric_input("risk_limit", "RR watch limit",
                  value = 1.8, min = 1, max = 5, step = 0.1)

# Outputs — these ids receive the result keys
mcp_text("memo"); mcp_table("evidence"); mcp_plot("risk_plot"); mcp_html("audit")
```

::: {.notes}
First real code, straight from the demo's Safety Signal Scout. The input ids — cohort, ae_term, grade_threshold, risk_limit — are deliberately the same names that become the tool's arguments; that is the names-match mapping contract from earlier (arg name == input id, the no-Shiny.js bridge). The output ids — memo, evidence, risk_plot, audit — are the result keys the function fills. Nothing exotic; ordinary Shiny inputs with one discipline: aligned names.
:::

## Code 2 — the tool is your reviewed function, declared

```r
tool <- ellmer::tool(
  fun = function(cohort = "All cohorts", ae_term = "Neutropenia",
                 grade_threshold = 3, risk_limit = 1.8) {
    # filter to cohort; event = AE grade >= grade_threshold; split by arm;
    # Haldane-corrected RR; small_cell flag; explicit decision thresholds
    screen_safety_signal_impl(cohort, ae_term, grade_threshold, risk_limit)
  },
  name = "screen_safety_signal",
  description = "Screen aggregate AE risk and return a guarded safety-review memo.",
  arguments = list(
    cohort          = ellmer::type_string("Cohort to screen."),
    ae_term         = ellmer::type_string("Adverse event term."),
    grade_threshold = ellmer::type_number("Minimum AE grade to count."),
    risk_limit      = ellmer::type_number("Relative-risk watch limit.")
  )
)
```

::: {.notes}
This is the reviewed-computation slide. The fun= body is ordinary R: filter to
cohort, mark events at the grade threshold, split by arm, Haldane-corrected
relative risk, explicit decision logic. That is the function you unit-test
today. ellmer::tool() gives it a name and declared arguments an MCP client can
call.
:::

## Code 3 — the result handoff: display + model_value

```r
list(
  memo = mcp_result_text(memo, model_value = list(   # <- data for the client
    widget = "Safety Signal Scout", cohort = cohort, ae_term = ae_term,
    risk_ratio = rr, risk_delta = risk_delta,
    decision = decision, small_cell = small_cell)),
  evidence  = mcp_result_table(evidence, text = "Aggregate AE evidence table."),
  risk_plot = mcp_result_plot(function() barplot(risk_counts),
                              model_value = risk_summary),
  audit     = mcp_result_html(audit)
)
```

::: {.notes}
Each result carries the rendered display the user sees and an optional
model_value: the data object the client receives separately. Note small_cell in
the result: the statistician-review flag is computed in R and travels as data.
The client does not parse the memo; it reads this list. Also note what is not
here: patient-level rows. The boundary is a property of what this function
returns.
:::

# Shiny integration {.section-divider background-color="#1b2f44"}

## Shiny and shinychat path: Shiny is the host {.runtime-slide}

```{=html}
<div class="runtime-visual">
  <div class="runtime-track">
    <div class="runtime-card is-blue">
      <span>01 SHINY SESSION</span>
      <strong>dashboard or shinychat</strong>
      <em>the parent app owns host state</em>
    </div>
    <div class="runtime-wire"><b>renders</b></div>
    <div class="runtime-card is-orange">
      <span>02 HOST SHELL</span>
      <strong><code>mcp_host_ui()</code> + iframe</strong>
      <em>HTML card loaded from <code>appHtml</code></em>
    </div>
    <div class="runtime-wire"><b>events</b></div>
    <div class="runtime-card is-green">
      <span>03 R TOOL</span>
      <strong>same <code>McpApp</code></strong>
      <em><code>app$call_tool()</code> in R</em>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="runtime-split is-two-paths">
    <div class="runtime-pane is-r">
      <span>SHINY DASHBOARD</span>
      <strong>Embed the live card</strong>
      <ul>
        <li><code>mcp_host_server()</code> registers host state</li>
        <li>iframe posts <code>tools/call</code> to the parent</li>
        <li>Shiny observer runs the R tool and replies</li>
      </ul>
    </div>
    <div class="runtime-pane is-chat">
      <span>SHINYCHAT</span>
      <strong>Return a tool-result card</strong>
      <ul>
        <li><code>as_shinychat_tool()</code> wraps the app as an ellmer tool</li>
        <li>tool result carries machine-facing value</li>
        <li>display extra contains the embedded live card</li>
      </ul>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="runtime-loop">
    <i>iframe bridge</i><i>Shiny.setInputValue</i><i>observeEvent</i><i>R computes</i><i>sendCustomMessage</i>
  </div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
This is the same architecture, but the host is now a Shiny session instead of a
desktop or IDE MCP client. The embedded card still has a JavaScript bridge. The
parent Shiny page has host JavaScript. Those two frames talk through
postMessage; the parent forwards events through Shiny's input bus. R handles
the tool call inside the active session. shinychat uses the same host machinery
inside a tool-result display.
:::

## Shiny and shinychat path: the details {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```r
app <- mcp_app(ui = ui, tools = list(tool),
               name = "rpharma-safety-signal")

# Shiny dashboard
mcp_host_ui("safety")
mcp_host_server("safety", app, trigger = "submit")

# shinychat
as_shinychat_tool(app)
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
- `mcp_host_server()` creates live host state in the Shiny session
- The card HTML is rendered into an iframe; there is no separate Shiny server inside the card
- Card JavaScript posts `tools/call` requests to the parent host
- Host JavaScript forwards those requests through `Shiny.setInputValue()`
- An R observer calls `mcp_host_call_tool()`, then sends the result back with `sendCustomMessage()`
- `as_shinychat_tool()` returns an ellmer tool whose display can include the same live card
- The same `model_value`/structured result is the machine-facing handoff
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the slide for Shiny developers. The parent Shiny app is the transport
and lifecycle owner. The iframe is a lightweight card view, not a nested Shiny
application. The live card can be embedded directly in a dashboard or returned
from a shinychat tool call. Either way, the same R tool computes and the same
result handoff is available for inspection.
:::

## Why Shiny remains useful

- Shiny is where many teams already review the workflow
- shinymcp lets the **same MCP App** run inside that app for adoption and testing
- The Shiny app can inspect the same result handoff an MCP client would receive

. . .

[Shiny provides a familiar review view for the same MCP contract.]{.takeaway}

::: {.notes}
Position Shiny precisely. It is the local review and adoption path. You can show
the card inside the dashboard, inspect the handoff, and let teams use a familiar
app while the same contract can be served to an MCP client.
:::

## Code 4 — one definition, multiple homes

```r
app <- mcp_app(ui = ui, tools = list(tool), name = "rpharma-safety-signal")

# Embed live in a Shiny dashboard:
mcp_host_ui("safety")
mcp_host_server("safety", app = app, trigger = "submit",
                initial_arguments = list(cohort = "Lung", ae_term = "Neutropenia"))

# Drop into a shinychat conversation:
as_shinychat_tool(app)

# Serve to an MCP client:
serve(app)
```

::: {.notes}
One definition, multiple client paths. The same McpApp embeds in the Shiny dashboard, wraps as an ellmer/shinychat tool, or serves over MCP. The active Shiny session owns host state and runs the tool in R; the iframe stays lightweight, no nested Shiny runtime per card.
:::

# Review boundaries {.section-divider background-color="#1b2f44"}

## What makes this reviewable?

:::: {.cardgrid}
::: {.gcard}
[01]{.gnum}[R computation]{.gtitle}[The tool body is the reviewed function.]{.gbody}
:::
::: {.gcard}
[02]{.gnum}[Declared schemas]{.gtitle}[The client fills declared slots; it cannot invent inputs.]{.gbody}
:::
::: {.gcard}
[03]{.gnum}[Aggregate boundary]{.gtitle}[Return aggregate evidence and audit metadata, not patient rows.]{.gbody}
:::
::: {.gcard data-accent="green"}
[04]{.gnum}[Result handoff]{.gtitle}[The client receives `model_value`, not copied page text.]{.gbody}
:::
::: {.gcard data-accent="orange"}
[05]{.gnum}[Human decision]{.gtitle}[Outputs support review; they do not replace accountability.]{.gbody}
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
These points come after the audience understands the integration. They are the
conditions under which an MCP client calling an R tool becomes reviewable. Be
explicit that aggregate-only is a property of the tool you write. shinymcp
provides the contract; validation and privacy design are still your process.
:::

## The handoff is explicit and logged

- The `model_value` from Code 3 is the unit of audit — structured data, not prose
- It can feed a meeting note, an audit log, or a downstream review workflow
- What never crosses the boundary is a property of what the function returns

```{=html}
<div class="dgm-split">
  <div class="dgm-node"><span class="k">TOOL RESULT</span><span class="t">One result</span></div>
  <div class="dgm-arr"><span class="ln"></span></div>
  <div class="dgm-split__branches">
    <div class="row">
      <div class="dgm-arr"><span class="lab">display · memo / table / plot</span><span class="ln"></span></div>
      <div class="dgm-node is-blue"><span class="k">HUMAN</span><span class="t">The human</span></div>
    </div>
    <div class="row">
      <div class="dgm-arr green"><span class="lab">model_value · data</span><span class="ln"></span></div>
      <div class="dgm-node is-green"><span class="k">MACHINE</span><span class="t">Client / log</span><span class="s">meeting note</span></div>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>
```

> The same `model_value` the client reads is the unit you audit, log, and route.

::: {.notes}
The same tool result yields a human-facing card and a client-facing data object.
The client does not parse prose; it reads the list. This is the difference
between dashboard interpretation and an inspectable contract.
:::

## The sandbox is not the whole data boundary

- MCP Apps are rendered as isolated app views in supporting clients
- Host and app communicate through a defined protocol conversation
- The data boundary still comes from **what your tool returns**
- Treat sandboxing as one layer, not a compliance certificate

::: {.notes}
This is the security caveat slide. Do not overclaim the iframe. In local Shiny
preview the iframe uses allow-scripts allow-same-origin, and different MCP
clients make different rendering choices. The data boundary is the aggregate-only
return contract plus the client's tool approval and logging behavior.
:::

# When to use it {.section-divider background-color="#1b2f44"}

## So — does it fit your workflow? {.smaller}

[We opened on when to use it. Now you've seen the mechanism, the code, and the demo — so you can actually answer it.]{.takeaway}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {style="border-left:5px solid #087443; padding-left:1rem;"}
**It fits**

- One named task — an `ellmer::tool` you call by name
- A fixed set of typed controls — dropdowns, numbers, sliders, checkboxes
- A returnable result — plot, table, text, HTML, or image, plus a `model_value`
- Reuse across surfaces — `serve()`, `mcp_host_server()`, `as_shinychat_tool()`
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {style="border-left:5px solid #ff7518; padding-left:1rem;"}
**It doesn't**

- Open-ended exploration — no single task to name with declared arguments
- It needs instant feedback — dragging a slider, brushing points, a live-streaming plot
- The interactive view *is* the deliverable — a rotatable 3-D plot, a hover-to-explore network
- State accumulates across steps — a multi-step wizard, not a one-shot call
:::
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the payoff to the "When to use shinymcp" slide, and it should feel
like a return, not a new topic. MCP Apps are strongest when the workflow is a
named operation with explicit arguments and a clear result; weakest when value
comes from continuous interaction, hidden session state, or an exploratory path
where the next operation is not defined. Invite the room to hold one of their own
apps against this list.
:::

## Why those are the limits

:::: {.cardgrid}
::: {.gcard}
[01]{.gnum}[Request / response]{.gtitle}[A card changes state by asking the host to call a tool.]{.gbody}
:::
::: {.gcard}
[02]{.gnum}[Explicit state]{.gtitle}[State lives in arguments, result data, or an external store — never a hidden session.]{.gbody}
:::
::: {.gcard}
[03]{.gnum}[No live session]{.gtitle}[This is not a Shiny session running inside the client.]{.gbody}
:::
::: {.gcard data-accent="green"}
[04]{.gnum}[UI is optional]{.gtitle}[The tool must still make sense when a client only calls it.]{.gbody}
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
This is the architecture behind the fit test, not a separate apology. MCP Apps
route meaningful changes through tool calls, so state has to be explicit and the
tool has to stand on its own without UI. That is exactly why open-ended,
high-frequency, or session-bound workflows are a poor fit — it is the shape of
the contract, and it is also what makes the contract inspectable.
:::

## The questions you're already asking

| Objection | Answer |
|---|---|
| "Why not just build for one client?" | Because MCP gives you an open contract you can reuse across clients |
| "Can this fit validation?" | The client supplies arguments; the **R tool** computes |
| "Will this leak patient data?" | Only return aggregate evidence; the boundary is in the tool contract |
| "Does every client render the UI?" | Tool calls are the stable part; interactive UI support is client-dependent |
| "What's the validation focus?" | Unit-test the R tools; inspect the JS bridge; assert `model_value` |

::: {.notes}
Pre-empt the room's real objections in their language so Q&A can go deeper. The
point is not a single-client integration; it is keeping R tools portable across
MCP clients. Then return to the same validation spine: R computes, the tool
returns aggregate data, and a human remains accountable.
:::

# Close {.section-divider background-color="#1b2f44"}

## When and why — the short version

[Reuse, don't rebuild: reviewed R stays the computation layer, exposed once as a declared contract that renders across MCP clients, Shiny, and shinychat.]{.takeaway}

::: {style="color:#39729e; font-weight:700; font-size:1.05em;"}
- **When:** bounded workflows, explicit inputs, an aggregate serializable result
- **Why it's reviewable:** declared schema in, `model_value` out, the round trip logged, a human still accountable
- **Why bother:** one contract instead of per-client glue — build once, reuse across clients
- **Not when:** open-ended exploration, interaction that needs instant feedback, or value that lives only in the live view
:::

::: {style="color:#455468; margin-top:1rem;"}
MCP standard · MCP App UI · shinymcp R adapter · Shiny review path
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the bookend to the early "When to use shinymcp" slide — same WHY
line, same when / not-when split, now earned by everything in between. Say it as
the one thing to remember: reuse, don't rebuild. R/Shiny tools can be served to
MCP clients without moving the computation out of R, and the declared contract is
what makes it reviewable. Then go to the install slide and Q&A.
:::
